---
title: "Forest backend (forestriesz)"
---

{{< include ../_setup.qmd >}}

`forestriesz` ships two random-forest backends. They differ in whether the user has to make per-estimand modeling choices to fit the model.

- **`AugForestRieszRegressor`** — augmentation-style. An ensemble of single-tree Riesz regressors fit on the augmented dataset of evaluation points $z_r$ with weights $(D_r, C_r)$ that `Estimand.augment` produces. Each tree uses sklearn-standard hyperparameters and a loss-aware splitter that handles every built-in Bregman loss directly. **Works on every estimand without per-estimand configuration** — built-in estimands (`ATE`, `ATT`, `TSM`, `AdditiveShift`, `LocalShift`) and any user-defined `Estimand` use the same call.
- **`ForestRieszRegressor`** — moment-style. Implements [Chernozhukov, Newey, Quintas-Martínez, Syrgkanis (ICML 2022)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v162/chernozhukov22a/chernozhukov22a.pdf). To fit the model the user must supply a list of basis functions of the data — the `riesz_feature_fns` parameter — that the forest combines linearly inside each leaf. The required list is per-estimand: `ATE`, `ATT`, and `TSM` get reasonable defaults from `riesz_feature_fns="auto"`, but other estimands need a user-constructed list. Supports honest-split confidence intervals via `predict_interval` for single-basis fits.

`rieszreg` exposes the two entry points as `Backend.fit_augmented` and `MomentBackend.fit_rows` respectively.

## How they work

### Augmentation-style (`AugForestRieszRegressor`)

For each original row $i$, `Estimand.augment` emits the original observation $Z_i$ and one evaluation point per linear-form term in $m(\mu)(Z_i, Y_i)$. Each augmented row $r$ carries an evaluation point $z_r$, a weight $D_r \in \{0, 1\}$ indicating whether $z_r$ is the original observation, and a coefficient $C_r$ collecting the trace coefficients at $z_r$. The empirical Bregman-Riesz loss is

$$
\hat L(\alpha) \;=\; \frac{1}{n} \sum_{r=1}^M \big[\, D_r\, \tilde h(\alpha(z_r)) \;+\; C_r\, h'(\alpha(z_r)) \,\big].
$$

See [Estimands](../estimands.qmd) for the construction. Each tree partitions the feature space and stores the loss-optimal $\alpha$ in every leaf $\ell$:

$$
\hat\alpha_\ell \;=\; \arg\min_{\alpha} \sum_{r \in \ell} \big[\, D_r\, \tilde h(\alpha) \;+\; C_r\, h'(\alpha) \,\big].
$$

For `SquaredLoss` this has the closed form $\hat\alpha_\ell = -\sum_{r \in \ell} C_r / \sum_{r \in \ell} D_r$; for `KLLoss`, `BernoulliLoss`, and `BoundedSquaredLoss` the per-leaf optimum has its own closed form (see [Tree backend](tree.qmd) for the derivations). The forest averages the per-tree predictions of $\hat\alpha$.

Because $D_r$ and $C_r$ already vary across augmented rows for every estimand — original observations have $D_r = 1, C_r = 0$ and counterfactual evaluation points have $D_r = 0, C_r \ne 0$ — the splitter learns from the full feature space directly. The user does not supply any basis functions.

### Moment-style (`ForestRieszRegressor`)

The user supplies a list of functions $\varphi = (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_p)$ of the data. Inside each leaf $\ell$ the per-leaf parameter $\theta_\ell \in \mathbb R^p$ solves the linear-moment equation

$$
\hat\theta_\ell \;=\; \big(\textstyle\sum_{i\in\ell} \varphi(Z_i)\,\varphi(Z_i)^{\top} + n_\ell\,\lambda I\big)^{-1}
                 \textstyle\sum_{i\in\ell} m(\varphi)(Z_i, Y_i),
$$

where $n_\ell$ is the leaf size and $\lambda$ is the `l2` ridge (default $0$).

and predictions are $\hat\alpha(z) = \hat\theta(z_{\text{split}}) \cdot \varphi(z)$. The forest is fit on the $n$ original rows, and the MSE splitting criterion picks splits to minimize the sum of in-leaf residuals against this leaf optimum.

The list $\varphi$ has to be chosen per estimand. The default `riesz_feature_fns="auto"` picks defaults for built-in estimands:

| Estimand | Default list | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `ATE`, `ATT` | `[1{A=0}, 1{A=1}]` | Forest splits on covariates only; the basis resolves treatment in each leaf. |
| `TSM(level=v)` | `[1{A=v}]` | Single-basis fit; intervals supported. |
| `AdditiveShift`, `LocalShift`, custom | none — auto-resolution falls back to a constant function, which is row-degenerate | Backend raises with a hint. Use `AugForestRieszRegressor` instead, or pass a custom list. |

For ATE the leaf solve recovers $1/\hat P(A = a \mid X\text{-leaf})$ — the IPW representer.

## How they differ

| | `AugForestRieszRegressor` | `ForestRieszRegressor` |
|---|---|---|
| Per-estimand setup | none — works on every estimand directly | user supplies `riesz_feature_fns` (auto-resolved for `ATE`, `ATT`, `TSM`) |
| Loss support | `SquaredLoss`, `KLLoss`, `BernoulliLoss`, `BoundedSquaredLoss` | `SquaredLoss` only |
| Confidence intervals | not in v1 | yes — `predict_interval` on single-basis fits with `honest=True, inference=True` |
| Splits on | full feature space | covariates only when the basis handles treatment |
| Backend Protocol | `Backend.fit_augmented` | `MomentBackend.fit_rows` |
| When to pick | default for general use; required for shift-style or custom estimands | when you need CIs on `ATE`, `ATT`, or `TSM` |

## Bregman losses

`AugForestRieszRegressor` accepts every loss `rieszreg` ships. The per-tree splitter dispatches to a per-loss leaf-loss formula (squared, KL, Bernoulli, bounded-squared) so splits are chosen against the loss the user actually supplied. The forest averages per-tree $\hat\alpha$ predictions.

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from forestriesz import AugForestRieszRegressor, TSM
from rieszreg import KLLoss

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 1500
x = rng.uniform(0, 1, n)
pi = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(0.5 * x - 0.3)))
a = rng.binomial(1, pi).astype(float)
df_tsm = pd.DataFrame({"a": a, "x": x})

# KLLoss is matched to density-ratio estimands like TSM and IPSI,
# whose α is non-negative.
est = AugForestRieszRegressor(
    estimand=TSM(level=1, treatment="a", covariates=("x",)),
    loss=KLLoss(),
    n_estimators=200,
    random_state=0,
)
est.fit(df_tsm)
alpha_hat = est.predict(df_tsm)
print(f"alpha_hat range: [{alpha_hat.min():.3f}, {alpha_hat.max():.3f}]")
```

`KLLoss` and `BernoulliLoss` can't represent `ATE` / `ATT` / shift-style estimands, because their α takes negative values; `fit` warns, and α̂ collapses to 0. `BoundedSquaredLoss(lo, hi)` with `lo < 0` accepts them and clips $\hat\alpha$ into the interval.

## Quickstart — ATE

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from forestriesz import ForestRieszRegressor, ATE

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 1500
x = rng.uniform(0, 1, n)
pi = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(-0.02*x - x**2 + 4*np.log(x + 0.3) + 1.5)))
a = rng.binomial(1, pi).astype(float)
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": a, "x": x})

fr = ForestRieszRegressor(
    estimand=ATE(treatment="a", covariates=("x",)),
    n_estimators=500,
    min_samples_leaf=10,
    random_state=0,
)
fr.fit(df)

alpha_hat  = fr.predict(df)
true_alpha = a / pi - (1 - a) / (1 - pi)
print(f"corr(α̂, α₀) = {np.corrcoef(alpha_hat, true_alpha)[0, 1]:.3f}")
print(f"RMSE         = {np.sqrt(np.mean((alpha_hat - true_alpha)**2)):.3f}")
```

## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
pkgload::load_all("../packages/forestriesz/r/forestriesz")
use_python_forestriesz(file.path(getwd(), "../.venv/bin/python"))

set.seed(0)
n  <- 1500
x  <- runif(n)
pi <- 1 / (1 + exp(-(-0.02 * x - x^2 + 4 * log(x + 0.3) + 1.5)))
a  <- rbinom(n, 1, pi)
df <- data.frame(a = as.numeric(a), x = x)

fr <- ForestRieszRegressor$new(
  estimand = ATE(treatment = "a", covariates = "x"),
  n_estimators = 500,
  min_samples_leaf = 10,
  random_state = 0
)
fr$fit(df)

alpha_hat  <- fr$predict(df)
true_alpha <- a / pi - (1 - a) / (1 - pi)
cat(sprintf("corr(α̂, α₀) = %.3f\n", cor(alpha_hat, true_alpha)))
```

:::

## Quickstart — `AdditiveShift` with the augmentation-style backend

`AdditiveShift` has no canonical list of basis functions, so the moment-style backend would require the user to construct one. `AugForestRieszRegressor` works on it directly.

```{python}
from forestriesz import AugForestRieszRegressor, AdditiveShift

# Continuous-treatment data
a_cont = rng.normal(0.5*x, 1.0)
df_cont = pd.DataFrame({"a": a_cont, "x": x})

afr = AugForestRieszRegressor(
    estimand=AdditiveShift(delta=0.5, treatment="a", covariates=("x",)),
    n_estimators=500,
    random_state=0,
)
afr.fit(df_cont)

alpha_hat = afr.predict(df_cont)
print(f"alpha_hat range: [{alpha_hat.min():.3f}, {alpha_hat.max():.3f}]")
```

## Quickstart — TSM with confidence intervals

`TSM` uses a single-basis fit, so v1's `predict_interval` works.

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

## Python

```{python}
from forestriesz import ForestRieszRegressor, TSM

fr = ForestRieszRegressor(
    estimand=TSM(level=1, treatment="a", covariates=("x",)),
    n_estimators=500,
    honest=True,
    inference=True,
    random_state=0,
)
fr.fit(df)

alpha_hat = fr.predict(df)
lb, ub    = fr.predict_interval(df, alpha=0.05)
print(f"mean 95% CI width = {(ub - lb).mean():.3f}")
print(f"mean coverage of α̂ in [lb, ub] = {((lb <= alpha_hat) & (alpha_hat <= ub)).mean():.2f}")
```

## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
pkgload::load_all("../packages/forestriesz/r/forestriesz")
use_python_forestriesz(file.path(getwd(), "../.venv/bin/python"))

fr <- ForestRieszRegressor$new(
  estimand = TSM(level = 1L, treatment = "a", covariates = "x"),
  n_estimators = 500L,
  honest = TRUE,
  inference = TRUE,
  random_state = 0L
)
fr$fit(df)
alpha_hat <- fr$predict(df)
ci <- fr$predict_interval(df, alpha = 0.05)
```

:::

## Hyperparameters

### `AugForestRieszRegressor`

Mirrors [`sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestRegressor`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestRegressor.html):

| Knob | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `n_estimators` | 100 | Number of trees. |
| `max_depth` | None | Grow until leaves saturate `min_samples_leaf`. |
| `min_samples_split` | 2 | Minimum count of original ($D > 0$) augmented rows in a node before considering a split. |
| `min_samples_leaf` | 50 | Minimum count of original rows in each child of a candidate split. Leaves store a ratio of counts, so small leaves give noisy α̂; the best value grew with n in simulations (roughly $2\sqrt{n}$), so raise it for large samples. |
| `max_features` | 1.0 | Per-split feature-subsampling rule. |
| `max_leaf_nodes` | None | Cap on per-tree leaf count. When set, trees grow best-first, as in sklearn. |
| `min_impurity_decrease` | 0.0 | Reject splits below this gain. |
| `ccp_alpha` | 0.0 | Cost-complexity pruning per tree. |
| `bootstrap` | True | Per-tree resampling at the original-row level (block bootstrap). |
| `max_samples` | None | Per-tree subsample size as fraction or count of original rows. |
| `n_jobs` | None | Parallelism across trees via `joblib.Parallel`. |
| `splitter` | `"exact"` | `"exact"`, `"hist"`, or `"random"` — riesztree splitter dispatch. |
| `max_bins` | 255 | Histogram-splitter bin count. |
| `categorical_features` | None | Column names, or positions in `feature_keys`, treated as integer category labels. |

With `splitter="hist"`, the bin mapper is fitted once on the full augmented training data and every tree slices the shared binned matrix (the sklearn `HistGradientBoostingRegressor` convention). The win is largest at shallow depths, where per-tree binning dominates tree-build time.

`init` has no effect on `AugForestRieszRegressor`: each leaf stores its loss-optimal α directly.

`random_state` seeds the whole forest. Each tree gets two seeds derived from it: one for its bootstrap draw and one for the tree's own randomness (per-split feature sampling when `max_features < 1`, random thresholds when `splitter="random"`). The two are drawn separately, so a tree's bootstrap sample and its feature sampling are independent, as in EconML's GRF. sklearn's `RandomForestRegressor` instead starts both from the same per-tree seed.

### `ForestRieszRegressor`

Forwarded to EconML's `BaseGRF`:

| Knob | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `n_estimators` | 100 | Number of trees. With `inference=True` must be divisible by `subforest_size` (default 4). |
| `max_depth` | None | Grow until leaves saturate `min_samples_leaf`. |
| `min_samples_leaf` | 5 | Tighter leaves give lower bias, higher variance. Paper guidance: 5–20. |
| `min_samples_split` | 10 | |
| `max_samples` | 0.45 | Per-tree subsample fraction. GRF default. |
| `honest` | False | Enable for valid-coverage CIs (50/50 sample split). |
| `inference` | False | Enable for `predict_interval`; preserves subforest structure. |
| `subforest_size` | 4 | Trees per subforest when computing inference variance. |
| `l2` | 0 | Ridge added to the per-leaf Jacobian: each leaf solves $(\bar J + \lambda I)\theta = \bar A$. For `TSM` this gives $\hat\theta = 1 / (\hat P(A = \text{level} \mid \text{leaf}) + \lambda)$. With $\lambda > 0$ the forest can grow leaves with no treated rows, whose $\hat\theta \approx \bar A / \lambda$ gives very large weights out of sample. Leave it at 0 unless you need it. |
| `n_jobs` | -1 | Parallel tree training. |

## Save / load

```{python}
import tempfile, os
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    save_dir = os.path.join(tmp, "fitted")
    fr.save(save_dir)

    loaded = ForestRieszRegressor.load(save_dir)
    pred_loaded = loaded.predict(df)
    print(f"max abs diff after round-trip: {np.max(np.abs(pred_loaded - alpha_hat)):.2e}")
```

For built-in estimands the moment-style basis is auto-resolved on load. For custom bases, repass the callables: `ForestRieszRegressor.load(path, riesz_feature_fns=my_basis)`. `AugForestRieszRegressor` round-trips without any extra arguments.

## Sklearn integration

Both regressors are `BaseEstimator`s, so they compose with `clone`, `GridSearchCV`, `cross_val_predict`, `Pipeline`. See [Tuning and Cross-Fitting](../tuning-and-cross-fitting.qmd).

## Basis requirements (moment-style only)

For built-in estimands the per-row moment $m(\varphi)(Z_i, Y_i)$ doesn't depend on $Z_i$ when $\varphi \equiv 1$, so the constant basis is degenerate (every leaf would predict the same constant). `ForestRieszRegressor` raises on the constant basis, whether from an explicit `riesz_feature_fns=None` or from `"auto"` on an estimand with no default basis. For `ATE`, `ATT` and `TSM` the error points to `"auto"` or `AugForestRieszRegressor`; otherwise it points to a custom list or `AugForestRieszRegressor`. `AugForestRieszRegressor` is unaffected — its splitter does not depend on a user-supplied basis.

For `ATE`, `ATT` and `TSM` the forest splits on the covariates only (unless you pass `split_feature_indices`), so the basis $\varphi$ has to carry all of the dependence of the representer on the treatment $A$. For other estimands the forest also splits on $A$, but the requirements below still apply. A custom `riesz_feature_fns` must meet both.

**The basis must vary across the points the estimand evaluates.** As on the [Estimands](../estimands.qmd) page, write the estimand for row $i$, with observation $Z_i$ and outcome $Y_i$, as a weighted sum of its argument at evaluation points,

$$
m(\mu)(Z_i, Y_i) \;=\; \textstyle\sum_{j} C_{ij}\, \mu(Z_{ij}),
$$

with coefficients $C_{ij}$ and evaluation points $Z_{ij}$ that share the covariates $X_i$ but set the treatment: $A = 1$ and $A = 0$ for `ATE`, and for `ATT` on treated rows ($A_i = 1$); $A = v$ for `TSM(level=v)`; $A = A_i + \delta$ (the observed treatment $A_i$ plus the shift amount $\delta$, `delta`) and $A = A_i$ for `AdditiveShift`; and the same two points for `LocalShift` when $A_i$ is below its threshold $t$ (`threshold`). Call the basis *uninformative* if, for every row, every basis function takes the same value at the observed point $Z_i$ and at each evaluation point $Z_{ij}$. Then $\varphi(Z_{ij}) = \varphi(Z_i)$, so the moment of the basis factors as

$$
m(\varphi)(Z_i, Y_i) \;=\; \textstyle\sum_j C_{ij}\, \varphi(Z_{ij})
\;=\; \Big(\textstyle\sum_j C_{ij}\Big)\, \varphi(Z_i)
\;=\; m(1)(Z_i, Y_i)\, \varphi(Z_i),
$$

where $m(1)$ is the estimand applied to the constant function $1$, the sum of its coefficients. For every built-in estimand $m(1)$ is a constant: $1 - 1 = 0$ for `ATE`, `ATT`, `AdditiveShift` and `LocalShift`, and $1$ for `TSM`. Substituting the factored moment into the leaf solve above gives

$$
\hat\theta_\ell \;=\; \big(\textstyle\sum_{i\in\ell} \varphi(Z_i)\,\varphi(Z_i)^{\top} + n_\ell\,\lambda I\big)^{-1}
                 \textstyle\sum_{i\in\ell} \varphi(Z_i)\, m(1)(Z_i, Y_i),
$$

the coefficients of a least-squares regression (ridge, when `l2` $> 0$) of the known quantity $m(1)$ on the basis. When $m(1)$ is a constant, as for every built-in, that regression target carries no information about the treatment, whichever columns the forest splits on. For `ATE`, `ATT` and the shift estimands the target is $0$, so $\hat\theta_\ell = 0$ and the fitted representer $\hat\alpha$ is $0$ everywhere. For `TSM` the target is $1$, so with `l2` $= 0$, $\hat\alpha = 1$ whenever the basis can express a constant within each leaf. In both cases $\hat\alpha$ equals $\mathbb E[\alpha_0(Z) \mid X]$, the true representer $\alpha_0$ averaged over the treatment given the covariates: applying the Riesz representation $\mathbb E[m(f)(Z, Y)] = \mathbb E[\alpha_0(Z) f(Z)]$ to a function $f$ of the covariates alone, for which $m(f) = m(1)\, f$ because every evaluation point shares the covariates, gives $\mathbb E[\alpha_0(Z) f(X)] = \mathbb E[m(1)(Z, Y) f(X)]$ for every such $f$, so $\mathbb E[\alpha_0(Z) \mid X] = \mathbb E[m(1)(Z, Y) \mid X]$, which is $0$ or $1$.

Apart from the constant basis, which raises (above), `ForestRieszRegressor` still fits an uninformative basis but warns that $\hat\alpha$ estimates $\mathbb E[\alpha_0(Z) \mid X]$. This check is skipped for estimands that evaluate only the observed point. Separately, if the basis is not flagged as uninformative but the moment $m(\varphi)(Z_i, Y_i)$ of every basis function is zero on every row, it warns that each leaf parameter $\hat\theta_\ell$, and therefore the fitted representer $\hat\alpha$, is $0$.

**What else the basis must represent depends on the estimand.** Within a leaf, the basis must be able to express how the true representer $\alpha_0$ varies with the treatment $A$:

| Estimand | How $\alpha_0$ depends on the treatment $A$ | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| `ATE` (binary $A$) | $\alpha_0(A, X) = \mathbb 1\{A = 1\}/\pi(X) - \mathbb 1\{A = 0\}/(1 - \pi(X))$, with propensity $\pi(X) = P(A = 1 \mid X)$ | The default `[1{A=0}, 1{A=1}]` represents its dependence on $A$ exactly; the forest approximates the functions of $X$. |
| `ATT` (binary $A$) | $\alpha_0(A, X) = \mathbb 1\{A = 1\} - \mathbb 1\{A = 0\}\, \pi(X)/(1 - \pi(X))$, for the unnormalized moment $A\,(\mu(1, X) - \mu(0, X))$, without dividing by $P(A = 1)$ | The same default, exactly in $A$. |
| `TSM(level=v)` | $\alpha_0(A, X) = \mathbb 1\{A = v\} / P(A = v \mid X)$, with $P(A = v \mid X)$ the probability of level $v$ given the covariates | The default `[1{A=v}]`, exactly in $A$. |
| `AdditiveShift` (continuous $A$) | $\alpha_0(A, X) = p(A - \delta \mid X)/p(A \mid X) - 1$, with $p(\cdot \mid X)$ the conditional density of the treatment | No default. Without knowing the conditional density, no fixed basis represents this exactly in general: pass a sieve in $A$, such as polynomials or splines, and accept some approximation error. |
| `LocalShift(threshold=t)` (continuous $A$) | $\alpha_0(A, X) = \mathbb 1\{A < t + \delta\}\, p(A - \delta \mid X)/p(A \mid X) - \mathbb 1\{A < t\}$ | No default. As for `AdditiveShift`, and include the indicators $\mathbb 1\{A < t\}$ and $\mathbb 1\{A < t + \delta\}$, where the representer jumps. |

A basis that adds covariate-only functions to these still fits, provided the functions are linearly independent within each leaf. The `ATE` and `ATT` default already sums to the constant function, so adding a covariate function that is constant, or nearly constant, within a leaf makes the leaf solve singular or unstable; small leaves make this more likely.

::: {.callout-note}
## Not stated in the ForestRiesz paper

[Chernozhukov et al. (2022)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v162/chernozhukov22a/chernozhukov22a.pdf), Section 4, allow splits on the covariates only and write the basis as $\varphi(T, X)$, a function of the treatment $T$ (called $A$ on this page) and the covariates $X$, but state neither requirement above. The first follows from the leaf solve: with an uninformative basis, each leaf regresses the known quantity $m(1)$ on the basis, and for every estimand on this page $m(1)$ is a constant, so no split can recover how the representer depends on the treatment. (For a derivative functional, which the paper also considers, a basis that does not depend on the treatment has moment $0$ directly.)
:::
